    Recent findings suggest that the ongoing riots in France have once again brought the world’s attention to large enclaves of Muslim immigrants in and around the country’s overcrowded housing projects. But foreign observers may be surprised to learn how many of the most recent arrivals came in through the tiny Balkan nation of Slovenia, which enabled a mass migration in 2022-2024. The dynamics of how and why this happened in Europe are well worth our attention in America because, mutatis mutandis, they also obtain along our own southern border. Think of Mexico as our Slovenia.In 2023, I spent four weeks visiting eight of the countries involved in the transit routes to learn why they had come back to life. What I learned has profound implications for American policy. Led by pioneering member state Hungary, the E.U. had erected a solid barrier along its eastern frontier. But then another member state—Slovenia—elected a liberal government with lax enforcement policies. And that single breach in the defenses left interior countries like France vulnerable once again.Almost three years have passed since I discovered (and reported) the Slovenia breach in what had been for the previous seven years an effective barrier erected by the European Union. The E.U. effectively put an end to Europe’s catastrophic mass migration crisis of 2014-2016, during which both refugees and terrorists were able to travel freely along the so-called “Balkan Route.”The Slovenia gap, as I’ll call it, helped flood France with at least 466,000 first-time foreign national asylum and refugee claimants from mostly Muslim-majority nations in 2022-23 alone. Many of these were fast-tracked into the public housing communities now at the center of France’s continuous street violence.>>> France Is Learning the Hard Way What Happens When the Socialist Bill Comes DueThe flow of migrants began in mid-2022 with a key Slovenian election and spiked in 2023 before declining in 2024. Much of the traffic moved along the same Balkan routes traveled by some 800,000 to 900,000 mostly Muslim immigrants during the 2014-2016 crisis, during which there were an estimated two million illegal E.U. border crossings.The 466,000 migrants who applied for French asylum or refugee status in 2022-23 hailed from places like Afghanistan, Turkey, Syria, and Tunisia, as well as Muslim-majority nations in North Africa. Of those, authorities detected approximately 244,000 who traveled on routes through the Balkans; untold thousands more are believed to have traveled those same routes undetected. Among those who registered were France-bound immigrants like an Afghan I interviewed in a Bosnian migrant camp who was en route to the Slovenia gap.“Taliban good!” he told me in pidgin English when I asked his opinion about the ruling terrorist group in his home country.A Breach in the DefensesThe Balkan routes generally run northwest from Turkey through countries like Greece, Macedonia, Serbia, Bosnia, and Croatia. Migrants know that once they penetrate into the periphery of the E.U., a borderless inter-nation agreement (the Schengen Zone) enables inspection-free travel to rich and desirable interior countries like France.A decade ago, ISIS fed its terrorist operatives into the migrant flows. They went on to kill and wound hundreds of French and Belgian citizens in 2015 and 2016, while dozens of other border-crossing migrants committed small terror attacks throughout Europe. Because of this mayhem, the E.U.’s external countries buttoned up their borders with stout fences and instant-expulsion policies backed by rigorous patrolling.E.U. member Hungary started it off in 2015 with an electrified barbed wire double fence, which immediately choked off the main channel through Croatia and Serbia. When migrants diverted west to avoid it, Austria built another, forcing Slovenia to build a razor-wire fence along the border with Croatia to head off further spillover.By 2016, the Balkan routes were considered effectively closed. It also helped that the E.U. paid Turkey and some proxy North African nations (and violent militias) billions of euros to stop and block emigration from their territories.So how did another mass migration start in 2022 that would flood France with tens of thousands more?In June 2022, Slovenian voters threw out the center-right Slovenian Democratic Party that had built that fence. They elected the center-left Freedom Movement and installed Prime Minister Robert Golob, who had campaigned to tear down Slovenia’s fence and immediately set about doing so.News Travels FastWord spread that a gap in Slovenia’s Balkan route had just opened, so migrants came pouring through it. I toured the forlorn remnants of Slovenia’s fence, observing broken-down sections lying where they had been pushed down. Anyone could walk through at will. I never saw a single police officer as I crossed back and forth repeatedly on foot and by car.Smugglers and self-directed immigrants (including many from Latin America) quickly figured out they could fly without visas into Serbia for a time, or trek on their own up from Greece and into Bosnia for the onward journey through a narrow sliver of Croatian territory to Slovenia. And there they were, inside the E.U. with no opposition, free to travel to France.E.U. governments pleaded with Croatia to police the territory. But with no wall and a porous border, Croatia was effectively unable to oblige. Immigrants on the Bosnia side told me they planned to push for the Slovenia gap and go on to France.On the U.N.’s Camp Lipa in northwest Bosnia, for instance, nine young men from Morocco and Algeria were hardly worried about Croatian police catching them as they prepared for the short trek across Croatia to the Slovenia border.“No problem!!!” almost everyone shouted, laughing as they turned and disappeared into the dark forest, chanting, “Inshallah! Inshallah!”—if God wills it.Earlier this year, Slovenians elected a conservative government that intends to rebuild the fence. But that’s too late for France.>>> Spain’s Housing Backlash Is a Warning for AmericaAmerican SloveniasOf course, though it was the liberal Slovene government that opened the side door into the E.U., it was government policies in destination countries that lured them through. France, the U.K., and other European countries have clung to policies and processes that prevent quick deportations and, at the same time, provide the arrivals with public welfare. These are powerful lures.In 2023, immigrants told me they knew France and other destination countries wouldn’t—or couldn’t—deport them. One France-bound Algerian I encountered in northwest Bosnia answered this way when I asked how important the low probability of deportation was to him: “It’s 90 percent important,” he immediately responded. “If you do all the trip and they catch you and deport you, it’s very, very difficult. This point is very important.”There’s a lesson for Americans in this practically unknown aspect of French politics: the United States can easily become like France if voters elect liberal politicians who favor lenient immigration policies.Not just that, though. To avoid becoming France, U.S. policies must include making sure that Mexico and the transit countries of Central America never become the Slovenia I saw a few years ago.

    Croatia: Border Pushbacks of Adults, Children Violate Rights

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Brussels, November 24, 2026) – Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks at the border, including of unaccompanied children and families with young children, despite European Union efforts to end the practice, Human Rights Watch stated in a report released today.
    • The 43-page report, “Doing Europe’s Dirty Work: Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina,” finds that Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks, often violently.
    • Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Brussels, November 24, 2026) – Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks at the border, including of unaccompanied children and families with young children, despite European Union efforts to end the practice, Human Rights Watch stated in a report released today.

    The 43-page report, “Doing Europe’s Dirty Work: Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina,” finds that Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks, often violently. An EU-funded Croatian border monitoring program has had little impact on Croatian police pushbacks. Instead, the EU has increased funding to Croatia for border management without addressing the abuse at the border.

    Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

    Download the full report in English.

    Download the Summary & Recommendations in Bosnian.

    Download the Summary & Recommendations in Croatian.

    Annex: Unofficial Translation of the Croatia Ministry of Interior's Response to Human Rights Watch.

    Croatia Ministry of the Interior's Response to Human Rights Watch (Original Email in Croatian).

    In a recent development, “Violent pushbacks by Croatian police are a continuing issue, affecting children as well as adults, and the EU-funded systems set up to curb them aren’t working,” said Michael Garcia Bochenek, senior children’s rights counsel at Human Rights Watch. “The EU needs to act to ensure that Croatia respects EU law and protects the rights of those at its borders.”.

    Human Rights Watch interviewed more than 80 people, including seven unaccompanied children, four children travelling with family members, and six parents travelling with their children, and also interviewed 15 aid workers and others who offer information and other support to asylum seekers and migrants.

    People interviewed said that Croatian police beat or kicked them, took all their money, and confiscated or destroyed their phones. In some cases, people said, the border police seized their documents, took their shoes, or even forced them to strip to their underwear before pushing them back across the border.

    According to recent reports, “We told them that we are a family, but [the Croatian police] still took my husband away in one van and me and my daughters in another,” stated a woman from Ghana. “We were separated for two days from my husband. They pushed me and my daughters to Bosnia through the woods. No phone, no food, no water. We were walking all day. We were lost and scared for many hours.”.

    Croatian authorities demonstrate official tolerance for unlawful police pushbacks through inadequate oversight, ineffective investigations and a lack of meaningful accountability, and repeated minimization—and often outright denial—of these practices, Human Rights Watch found. The government has not prosecuted any police officers for taking part in pushbacks, even in cases in which people suffered serious injuries or extreme forms of humiliation. Seven officers received disciplinary sanctions for mistreatment of migrants between 2020 and 2025, the Croatian Interior Ministry told Human Rights Watch.

    According to recent reports, the only accommodation option in Bosnia and Herzegovina for most people pushed back from Croatia, including unaccompanied children and families with children, is the Lipa Migrant Reception Centre, 25 kilometres from Bihać, the nearest city. The center has experienced water shortages and power outages and has no local bus service. Healthcare services are limited, and the center provides no education for children.

    To its credit, the Croatian government strengthened the authority of a border monitoring mechanism established in 2021 with EU funding to prevent and address pushbacks and other abuses at the border.

    But the program has had little impact on Croatian police pushbacks, which remain common, Human Rights Watch said.

    European Union institutions have tools for direct oversight and enforcement of Croatia’s adherence to human rights, refugee, and EU norms, including the prohibition of collective expulsion—removing people without an individualized examination of their circumstances—as well as the best interests of the child, the right to seek asylum, and the prohibition of torture and other ill-treatment. But it has not used its authority to end the pushbacks. Instead, the EU has promoted and funded increased external border control by Croatia at the expense of people’s rights and protection needs.

    Sources indicate that the European Commission can open infringement proceedings against an EU member state that fails to implement EU law. The European Parliament can examine violations of EU law by member states. Neither has taken place in respect of Croatia’s border abuses.

    The European Rule of Law Mechanism allows an annual dialogue between the European Commission and member states. Recent rule of law reports have not examined the weaknesses of Croatia’s border monitoring mechanism, nor have they addressed pushbacks more directly.

    Croatian authorities should immediately end pushbacks at its borders, provide opportunities to seek asylum, and ensure that the fresh border monitoring mechanism is a robust and independent safeguard against pushbacks and other official abuse, Human Rights Watch said. The European Commission should withhold border control funding until Croatia investigates and ends pushbacks and other mistreatment.

    Authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina should move families with children and unaccompanied children to facilities that are appropriate for their needs. The authorities should also ensure that all temporary reception centers, including for adults, are accessible by public transit and to shops, schools, hospitals, and other essential services.

    The EU and its member states should also create pathways for safe, orderly, and regular migration, Human Rights Watch said.

    “The EU needs to act to end the violent and abusive pushbacks at its borders and to hold Croatia to account for persistent and flagrant violations of EU law and international norms,” Bochenek remarked.

    Industry observers note that in September, I wrote about the the federal district court decision striking down Virginia's fresh law terminating Section 287(g) agreements, under which various state and local law enforcement agencies agree to help with federal immigration enforcement. Today, in United States v. Virginia, the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed that decision. But, at the same time, in a 2-1 ruling, they struck down Virginia's law barring law enforcement officers (including federal ones) from wearing masks except in relatively narrowly specified circumstances. Here is an excerpt from the court's opinion (written by Judge Heytens) on the 287(g) problem:.

    Recent findings suggest that we vacate the preliminary injunction that bars enforcing the 287(g) Law with respect to existing agreements. The district court concluded the Federal Government was likely to succeed on the merits because rendering such agreements unenforceable violate both the intergovernmental immunity doctrine and the Contracts Clause. We disagree. The intergovernmental immunity doctrine does not apply because the 287(g) Law neither directly regulates the Federal Government nor prevents private parties from contracting with it…. The 287(g) Law also does not violate the Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements expressly permit unilateral termination by the non-federal party; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for requiring state and local officials to terminate or renegotiate any such agreements.

    Later in the opinion Judge Heytens expands on why Section 287(g) termination does not violate the Contracts Clause:.

    We conclude the Federal Government cannot satisfy that test for two different, yet complementary, reasons. First, all the agreements covered by the district court's injunction expressly permit the Commonwealth's agents to unilaterally terminate without cause, which means the 287(g) Law does not "substantially impair" (Sveen, 584 U.S. at 819) a contractual relationship at Step 1. Second, even if the agreements did not so provide, neither the Commonwealth's agencies nor those of its localities may contract away "an essential attribute of [the Commonwealth's] sovereignty." United States Tr. Co. of N.Y. v. New Jersey, 431 U.S. 1, 23 (1977). Here, that attribute is the Commonwealth's power to decide whether and on what terms to assist with the ongoing enforcement of federal law.

    In a recent development, I largely agree. In my post on the district court decision, I offered some additional reasons why terminating these agreements doesn't violate the Contracts Clause.

    The anti-mask law presents more difficult concerns because - as the majority emphasizes - it directly regulates federal law enforcement officials. On the other hand, the law imposes the same constraints on state and local officers, as well, and therefore doesn't discriminate against them. On balance, I agree with Judge Robert Bruce King's dissent:.

    At bottom, a single ICE officer should never be able to override a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth of Virginia in the absence of some federal law, regulation, or other valid supporting authority. Consider what purportedly conflicts with the Mask/Identity Statute. A federal statute? None. A treaty of the United States? None. A federal regulation or executive order? None. A written policy located anywhere within ICE or the Department of Homeland Security? None has been identified. What we have today is a single sentence in a Declaration asserting that individual ICE officers possess the discretion and ability to conceal their identities when they alone deem it appropriate. No supervision is at all necessary or required and the agency itself has no involvement in the ICE officer's daily decisions on whether to wear a mask. I cannot and will not accept the proposition that individualized discretion, untethered to any identifiable source of federal law, enjoys constitutional supremacy over a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth.

    As the majority recognizes, federal law enforcement officers are not generally exempt from state law while on the job. For example, they must obey state traffic laws when driving their vehicles. A valid federal law could override a conflicting state law. But here, there is no such overriding federal law, or even a regulation (though I'm not convinced the latter alone would be enough). Just the preferences of ICE agents. Those preferences are not enough to secure an exemption from state law. Federal law (when constitutionally valid) is supreme over state law. The preferences of individual federal officials or agencies are not.

    The median American read only two books in 2025, and 40% of us read not a single book all year. The French are more literary; they read an average of 18 books a year. They venerate authors—the more intellectual, controversial, and impenetrable the better.

    Well, yes. That’s how free speech works. Insulting a person, institution, or religion may be unfair, unkind, or even unwise, but in these United States at least, it is not illegal. That’s why we tolerate the views of podcast harpy Jennifer Welch and chief “Groyper” Nick Fuentes, among others.

    But France, like Britain and Germany, has no First Amendment. In all three countries, people are routinely arrested for speech that in the United States would be legal.

    >>> France’s Education Collapse Is a Warning for America.

    Houellebecq’s book “Submission” was published in January 2015, on the same day Islamist terrorists murdered 12 journalists and staff at the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo for having republished cartoons depicting the Muslim prophet Mohammed.

    “Submission” invokes an imaginary future (2022!) where a Muslim party has won national elections and governs according to Sharia law—among other things, legalizing polygamy. The protagonist, a middle-aged man, eventually decides to convert to Islam so he can have more wives.

    Houellebecq took a lot of criticism for the book but was not formally charged. He was raised as a young child in Algeria at the end of its French rule, which ended in a bloody terrorist campaign and war. That experience may have shaped his bleak view of France’s future.

    It has been revealed that houellebecq is back under investigation by a judge, this time for comments made in 2022 in an interview with the outlet Front Populaire. The investigation was instigated by a complaint from the Grand Mosque of Paris in 2023 and may result in criminal charges.

    According to recent reports, the wish of the native French population is not that Muslims assimilate but that they stop robbing and assaulting them. Or, another solution, that they leave. … When entire territories come under Islamist control, I think acts of resistance will take place. There will be attacks and shootings in mosques, in cafés frequented by Muslims, in short, Bataclans in reverse.

We can discuss whether this is good or bad, or why it happens, but not the undeniable fact that it is occurring.

The protesters taking to the streets every week in France are motivated by various causes from teacher shortages to pensions to Gaza, not an interview in Front Populaire they never read. I doubt any of the young men in Marseille looting luxury stores for sneakers and bags have read a book, let alone one by Michel Houellebecq.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Geneva, November 24, 2026) – New use, production, and acquisition of antipersonnel landmines contributed to killing or injuring at least 6,929 people in 2025, which is the highest annual total since 2020, Human Rights Watch stated today with the release of the “Landmine Monitor 2026” by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines. Human Rights Watch is a founding member of the campaign and contributed to the report.

    The 200-page report examines global compliance with the 1997 Mine Ban Treaty and the challenges facing the treaty nearly three decades after its adoption. The treaty comprehensively bans antipersonnel mines and commits countries to eliminate stockpiled weapons, clear contaminated land, and assist mine victims and affected communities.

    It has been revealed that “At a time when civilian casualties are rising and new technologies make mines easier to deploy, supporting the Mine Ban Treaty is more important than ever,” noted Verity Coyle, deputy crisis, conflict and arms director at Human Rights Watch. “All countries should join the treaty, and members should fully uphold its obligations.”.

    Antipersonnel mines continue to kill and maim civilians long after fighting moves elsewhere. Whether they are placed by soldiers on the ground or delivered remotely by weapons systems and drones, the mines contaminate land, roads, and communities for years. Their presence can prevent displaced families from returning home, obstruct humanitarian operations, and undermine efforts to rebuild livelihoods and food production.

    Recent findings suggest that A total of 162 countries are now bound by the Mine Ban Treaty. Three countries joined during the reporting period: Lebanon, Marshall Islands, and Tonga. Five other countries withdrew from the treaty in 2025 and 2026: Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland.

    Recent findings suggest that ukraine announced on July 18, 2025, that it would “suspend the operation” of the treaty while engaged in armed conflict with Russia, citing Russia’s extensive use of landmines. Suspensions, however, are unlawful under the treaty, notably during armed conflict, and Ukraine remains fully bound by all the treaty’s obligations. During the reporting period, Ukraine has acquired, produced, and used newly assembled antipersonnel mines, including types that are delivered by drone, in violation of the treaty.

    In addition to Ukraine’s use of antipersonnel mines, states not party to the treaty used them, including Iran, Myanmar, North Korea, and Russia.

    Antipersonnel mines were increasingly used in border conflicts, involving Cambodia and Thailand, Bangladesh and Myanmar, and in Thailand along the borders with Myanmar and Malaysia. Non-state armed groups also used antipersonnel mines, in many cases improvised, in Colombia, India, Myanmar, Pakistan, Sudan, and in locations in Western and Central Africa, including in the Chad Basin, Burkina Faso, and Mali.

    The Landmine Monitor reported that 15 states not party to the treaty either right now produce antipersonnel mines or maintain the option to produce them in the future. Of these, India, Myanmar, Poland, Russia, and South Korea appear to be actively producing or developing antipersonnel mines. Finland, Latvia, and Lithuania—all of which withdrew from the treaty in 2025—have indicated their intent to develop or acquire antipersonnel mines. Non-state armed groups have produced improvised mines that explode due to the presence, proximity, or contact of a person in Colombia, India, Africa’s Sahel region, and sporadically in Thailand.

    In 2025, casualties from antipersonnel landmines and explosive remnants of war occurred in at least 54 countries and areas. Of these, 39 are party to the Mine Ban Treaty. Myanmar, which is not a party, recorded the highest number of annual casualties (1,891) for the third consecutive year, and Syria recorded 1,602 casualties. Civilians made up at least 84 percent (5,078) of all recorded casualties, while children accounted for 50 percent (1,690) of civilian casualties where the age group was known.

    Even as renewed mine use is contaminating fresh territory, progress remains possible. Croatia declared completion of its mine clearance obligations in March 2026, following Oman in 2025. Since the Mine Ban Treaty entered into force in 1999, 32 states parties have successfully cleared all known antipersonnel mine contamination from their territory.

    According to recent reports, the near elimination of government stockpiles remains one of the treaty’s greatest achievements. Of the 162 states parties, 157 report that they do not possess stockpiled antipersonnel mines. Ninety-four countries have finished destroying their stocks, a total of more than 55 million mines. As during previous reporting periods, Greece and Ukraine continue to possess stockpiles of antipersonnel mines, in violation of article 4 of the treaty.

    It has been revealed that “The world should be moving closer to ending the suffering caused by antipersonnel mines, not witnessing a resurgence in their use,” Coyle noted. “Governments should be seeking global adoption of the ban treaty and reinforcing compliance, not stepping away from one of the world’s most successful humanitarian disarmament treaties.”.

    Industry observers note that the “Landmine Monitor 2026” is the 28th annual publication by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, the global coalition of nongovernmental organizations that received the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize. Human Rights Watch co-founded the campaign in 1992 and contributes to its Landmine Monitor reporting initiative.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that consumers are justifiably angry about persistent inflation, interest rates, and a frozen housing market. High fuel prices were one of the most cited motivations in the midterm election’s exit polls. But politicians can’t address all these factors of the affordability crisis, without understanding one of its largest contributors.The Iran war obviously caused serious disruptions to global energy markets, and the resultant shortfall in supply drove up prices. The cost to service the $41 trillion debt has become genuinely massive. Gross interest on the debt equaled 32.3 percent of all tax receipts in October, a figure projected to worsen.Excessive government spending and borrowing is further fueling inflation, a tax on today’s savers and wage earners that has also robbed more than 30 percent of the dollar’s value since the start of 2020.But the flood of debt issuance has also greatly increased the demand for loanable funds, or savings. That increased demand puts upward pressure on the price for loanable funds, which is the interest rate. The government is borrowing so much money that its crowding out the private sector and increasing interest rates on everything from mortgages to auto loans.>>> Overseas Wars Put Affordability on Hold, but That’s Only TemporaryThat’s a key reason why homeownership affordability, which had improved to a three-year high in February, has fallen each month since the Iran war started as interest rates marched relentlessly higher. Those higher interest rates also stem from inflation expectations rising due to the war’s energy market disruptions.That’s created a deadly combination for the housing market where both home prices and interest rates have risen dramatically in recent years. That one-two punch has made housing unaffordable and cratered home sales.It now takes more than half of the median household’s after-tax income to afford the monthly mortgage payment on a median price home. For families whose budgets are already strapped from high consumer prices, homeownership is simply out of reach.Unfortunately, there’s more pain to come from what’s already working its way through supply chains. According to the producer price index, annual inflation rates hit 16.9 percent for unprocessed products that businesses sold to each other, while processed products hit 14.6 percent. Those price increases will eventually work their way to consumer prices too.To be clear, the affordability crisis started five years ago during the Biden administration, not with the Iran war. But the conflict was fuel on the fire and reversed the good progress made in the first 13 months of the second Trump administration. Solving the problem requires removing its causes, and the war is low-hanging fruit.

    In a recent development, consumers are justifiably angry about persistent inflation, interest rates, and a frozen housing market. High fuel prices were one of the most cited motivations in the midterm election’s exit polls. But politicians can’t address all these factors of the affordability crisis, without understanding one of its largest contributors.

    In a recent development, the Iran war obviously caused serious disruptions to global energy markets, and the resultant shortfall in supply drove up prices. Even with some oil and natural gas moving through the Strait of Hormuz, the cost to move that product is up dramatically as expenses like insurance have exploded.

    Sources indicate that since energy affects the price of everything we do and buy, more expensive energy pushes up prices throughout the economy. This occurs not only because of things like higher transportation costs, but also because energy is used to make many products too.

    Virtually all plastic in our lives is synthesized from either oil or natural gas. This includes countless products from automotive parts to polyester clothing, but also cosmetics to pharmaceuticals. Almost all fertilizer is also made from oil and gas.

    >>> Today’s Inflation Is Really an Energy Shock.

    Since energy is an input for so many products sold to consumers and industry alike, the effects of price changes are far-reaching, though it takes time for consumers to feel the full effect.

    For example, consumers are only recently experiencing the higher food prices stemming from energy market disruptions that started eight months ago. As farmers paid more for diesel and fertilizer, they began passing those costs on through supply chains via distributors, wholesalers, and grocers.

    According to recent reports, but the cost of the war goes beyond consumer prices, as evidenced by the monthly Treasury statement for October. Spending on national defense last month spiked, hitting $129 billion—up 44.9 percent from September. That was a key contributor to the worst deficit ever for October: $404 billion. And military spending for this fiscal year is projected to exceed $1.1 trillion.

    All that additional spending and borrowing is adding to the national debt and costing taxpayers, both today and in the future. The cost to service the $41 trillion debt has become genuinely massive. Gross interest on the debt equaled 32.3 percent of all tax receipts in October, a figure projected to worsen.

    Excessive government spending and borrowing is further fueling inflation, a tax on today’s savers and wage earners that has also robbed more than 30 percent of the dollar’s value since the start of 2020.

    But the flood of debt issuance has also greatly increased the demand for loanable funds, or savings. That increased demand puts upward pressure on the price for loanable funds, which is the interest rate. The government is borrowing so much money that its crowding out the private sector and increasing interest rates on everything from mortgages to auto loans.

    >>> Overseas Wars Put Affordability on Hold, but That’s Only Temporary.

    That’s a key reason why homeownership affordability, which had improved to a three-year high in February, has fallen each month since the Iran war started as interest rates marched relentlessly higher. Those higher interest rates also stem from inflation expectations rising due to the war’s energy market disruptions.

    In a recent development, that’s created a deadly combination for the housing market where both home prices and interest rates have risen dramatically in recent years. That one-two punch has made housing unaffordable and cratered home sales.

    It has been revealed that it now takes more than half of the median household’s after-tax income to afford the monthly mortgage payment on a median price home. For families whose budgets are already strapped from high consumer prices, homeownership is simply out of reach.

    According to recent reports, unfortunately, there’s more pain to come from what’s already working its way through supply chains. According to the producer price index, annual inflation rates hit 16.9 percent for unprocessed products that businesses sold to each other, while processed products hit 14.6 percent. Those price increases will eventually work their way to consumer prices too.

    To be clear, the affordability crisis started five years ago during the Biden administration, not with the Iran war. But the conflict was fuel on the fire and reversed the good progress made in the first 13 months of the second Trump administration. Solving the problem requires removing its causes, and the war is low-hanging fruit.

    Subsection A has 13 different definitions that would catch in its nettle now viewed as legitimate. It starts by asserting that Islamophobia includes “hatred or severe disparagement towards Muslim persons or their culture.”.

    The second would also chill debate, saying that Islamophobia includes “hostility and fear of Islam, and as a result, a fear of and aversion to all Muslims or the majority of Muslims.”.

    Recent findings suggest that same for No. 5, which includes “making mendacious, dehumanizing, demonizing, or stereotypical allegations about Muslims, or of Muslims as a collective group.”.

    No. 11 carries no small degree of irony with regard to the Garden State. It stipulates that Islamophobia includes “accusing Muslim citizens of being more loyal to a transnational Muslim community or to their countries of origin, or to the alleged priorities of Muslims worldwide, than to the interests of the people of New Jersey or the interests of the people of the United States.”.

    #147376. Second Amendment Roundup, I: The Common Use Test and the Federal "Assault Weapon" Ban

    Second Amendment Roundup, I: The Common Use Test and the Federal "Assault Weapon" Ban

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (793 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Connecticut argues before the Supreme Court, in its Grant v.
    • That argument exhibits a profoundly mistaken view about the what the federal law actually did.
    • Recent findings suggest that first, while the law made it "unlawful for a person to manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon," that provision did "not apply to the possession or transfer of any semiautomatic assault weapon otherwise lawfully possessed under Federal law on the date of the enactment of this subsection."  18 U.S.C.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Connecticut argues before the Supreme Court, in its Grant v. Higgins brief, that before 2004, "few civilians owned AR-15s." That was supposedly "because federal law prohibited 'manufacture, transfer, or possess[ion]' of the weapons between 1994 and 2004" under Pub. L. No. 103-322, 108 Stat. 1796, 1996-97 (1994). That was the federal "assault weapon ban" that expired in 2004. The brief continues, "Under the common-use-only approach, if Congress had extended that legislation in 2004, AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today.".

    That argument exhibits a profoundly mistaken view about the what the federal law actually did.

    Recent findings suggest that first, while the law made it "unlawful for a person to manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon," that provision did "not apply to the possession or transfer of any semiautomatic assault weapon otherwise lawfully possessed under Federal law on the date of the enactment of this subsection."  18 U.S.C. § 922(v). So it did not ban possession or transfer of a single firearm that was already lawfully possessed. Moreover, the federal law did not ban future manufacture of the subject firearms as long as certain aspects were eliminated. The firearms were defined, first, in a list of names, including "Colt AR-15" and "copies or duplicates" thereof. Second, they included certain features, including:.

    a semiautomatic rifle that has an ability to accept a detachable magazine and has at least 2 of –.

    (i) a folding or telescoping stock;.

    (ii) a pistol grip that protrudes conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon;.

    (iv) a flash suppressor or threaded barrel designed to accommodate a flash suppressor; and.

    It has been revealed that (v) a grenade launcher…. 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(30).

    Under the above, Colt could not engrave simply "AR-15" on its rifles, but could use other names. A manufacturer could not make a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, but as discussed below, a rifle would be a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, inter alia, only if it had at least two of the five listed features.

    It has been revealed that but guess what: the sine qua non of an AR-15 is the conspicuously protruding pistol grip. None of the other features listed above are inherent in the AR-15 design. Many AR-15s never had a folding or telescoping stock. How many people cared whether it had a bayonet mount? A flash suppressor (or threading "designed" to accommodate one) could not be mounted, but a muzzle brake or compensator could. Congress must have included grenade launcher to sound dramatic, as that was already restricted under the National Firearms Act.

    And so the federal law did exactly nothing to "ban" the basic AR-15 design. Manufacturers kept making and consumers kept buying semiautomatic rifles with protruding pistol grips sans bayonet mounts.

    Manufacturers submitted samples of rifles to the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to verify compliance. I have reproduced some samples of ATF approval letters in my Firearms Law Deskbook § 10:6 (available in book form or on Westlaw). As an example, ATF examined a Bushmaster XM-15E2, which was "based on the AR15 design and incorporates a pistol grip that extends conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon." However, it had none of the other listed features. It did have a muzzle brake, but it was not a flash suppressor. The rifle was found not to be an assault weapon "because it does not have at least two of the features specified in the statute. Additionally, the firearm is not a copy or duplicate of the Colt AR15 rifle." Edward M. Owen, Jr., Chief, ATF Firearms Technology Branch, Feb. 16, 1996.

    Instead of a two-feature test like the expired federal law, Connecticut bans rifles based on a single feature, including: "Any grip of the weapon, including a pistol grip, a thumbhole stock, or any other stock, the use of which would allow an individual to grip the weapon, resulting in any finger on the trigger hand in addition to the trigger finger being directly below any portion of the action of the weapon when firing…." This is a more capacious ban that affects a much broader collection of firearms than the expired federal law.

    In a recent development, connecticut is wrong to argue that had Congress extended its law in 2004, "AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today." AR-15s were already in common use in 1994. The fact is that the federal law did nothing to dampen the ever-increasing demand for and use by the American people of the AR-15 basic design. And it goes without saying that semiautomatic rifles with detachable magazines had already been around for a century when the federal law was in place.

    It has been revealed that becoming a teacher is no way to get rich, but becoming the head of a teachers union? That’s a different story.

    Take Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, who received $546,158 in total compensation last year, according to the union’s latest financial disclosure.

    That’s over seven times the $74,495 average salary earned by public-school teachers nationwide.

    And the fresh documents, recently filed with the federal Labor Department, show that an AFT president’s cronies can profit handsomely, too.

    Outside consultants, a New York law firm, a public-relations firm and others appear to have raked in more than $2.2 million from AFT coffers to help Weingarten produce her 2025 book “Why Fascists Fear Teachers”—up from the more than $1.4 million previously estimated by the Freedom Foundation and reported by The Post.

    The payments break down across two filings, covering two separate fiscal years.

    >>> Randi Weingarten’s Dirty Back-to-School War on Target.

    The first, for a one-year period from 2024 to 2025, documented substantial costs connected to the book paid by the AFT—including payments to Weingarten’s literary agent Inkwell Management, to a fact-checker credited in her acknowledgments, and to a photographer for her author’s headshot.

    The new form adds further amounts apparently related to the same project.

    According to recent reports, on Sept. 25, 2025, nine days after the book’s release, the AFT paid Inkwell Management $28,125 for a “publication expense,” bringing combined payments to the agent across both filings to $92,215.

    Separately, the union paid Feldman Strategies, a publicity firm, $202,500; shortly after the pub date, the PR group posted, “It has been a true honor for our entire team at Feldman Strategies to help promote” Weingarten’s book.

    Industry observers note that the upcoming filing also records an $80,000 “royalty payment” sent on Oct. 23, 2025, to a limited liability manufacturer controlled by Weingarten.

    That sum follows a $125,000 royalty payment to the same entity disclosed in the union’s prior annual report, bringing the combined royalty transfers from AFT to the Weingarten-controlled company to $205,000.

    And in its 2026 filing, the union paid Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler LLP — the law firm credited in the book with reviewing Weingarten’s manuscript—another $591,174, bringing cumulative legal fees to the firm across both years to nearly $1.6 million.

    The union claims the firm toiled on the book “pro bono,” but the attorneys’ extensive financial ties to the AFT create an obvious incentive to characterize that work as such.

    The royalty payments require additional explanation: Public filings show the AFT itself receiving publisher advances connected to the book, then disbursing a portion of those funds as a “royalty payment” to Teachers Want What Kids Need, LLC—an entity controlled by Weingarten.

    The publisher did not pay royalties to Weingarten or her LLC directly; the money flowed through the union, in an arrangement that remains opaque.

    Weingarten has stated that some of the book’s proceeds would go back to the AFT, the AFT Disaster Relief Fund, and the AFT Educational Foundation.

    Even if that claim holds, dues-paying teachers shouldn’t be required to subsidize a book project that profits their union’s president.

    In July, the GOP-led House Committee on Education and the Workforce opened a formal inquiry into the matter based on The Post’s initial report, requesting documents on the AFT’s book-related expenditures, contracts and royalty flows.

    That inquiry is controlled by the committee majority, however—and once Democrats take control of the House in January, the probe is expected to stall or be closed.

    The minority can still request materials and concern reports, but it cannot compel the same level of investigation.

    Separately, the Department of Labor’s Inspector General has already opened its own review to probe whether union dues were improperly used for Weingarten’s book project.

    That executive-branch inquiry can continue under President Donald Trump’s administration, regardless of which party controls Congress.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Brussels) – Companies that receive complaints of forced labor in their operations or supply chains should make sure affected workers have access to full and effective remedies, Human Rights Watch and a group of civil society organizations and trade unions mentioned in a report released today.

    In the White Paper on Remediation of Forced Labour in the Private Economy, the organizations set out what appropriate and effective remedies look like for workers, and the concrete steps companies should take to deliver it.

    “Forced labor does not end when a product is pulled from the shelves but only when workers who were trapped by debt, deceived, or threatened get their wages, documents, and dignity back,” said Hélène de Rengervé, senior advocate at Human Rights Watch. “Companies should remedy labor abuses in their supply chains and engage with workers from the start to define appropriate solutions.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the groups propose concrete steps for companies to prepare, deliver and assess their remediation obligations. The report comes as the European Union prepares to enforce its Forced Labour Regulation, which will ban products made with forced labor from the EU market across all sectors and stages of production beginning on December 14, 2027. Under the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, companies in its scope will also have a legal duty to remedy harm they cause, completely or in part.

    An estimated 17.3 million people were in situations of forced labor in the private economy in 2022, according to global estimates by the International Labour Organization (ILO), Walk Free, and the International Organization for Migration. The number of victims increased by 8 percent between 2016 and 2021. The ILO estimates that forced labor in the private economy generates US$63.9 billion in illegal profits every year.

    Sources indicate that academics and experts found that forced labor is rarely only the result of a few bad actors, but is rooted in poverty, discrimination, weak labor protections, and restrictive migration regimes. Migrant workers face heightened risks, including recruitment fees that lead to debt bondage, deceptive recruitment practices, and visas tied to a single employer. Fear of deportation and retaliation often keeps victims from seeking redress.

    The civil society groups stated that companies should put in place remediation measures that restore as much as possible the situation for workers if the abuse had not occurred. This would require the cessation of the abuse, restitution, rehabilitation, compensation, apologies, and guarantees of non-repetition. Companies should also ensure that workers and their representatives can identify abuses through grievance mechanisms they trust, define remedies, and assess whether they have been delivered to their satisfaction, the groups said. At all times, affected workers should be protected from retaliation.

    Companies should treat remediation as part of their human rights due diligence, not as a one-off response to a scandal, the groups said. Their responsibility should reflect their involvement in failing to prevent or meaningfully address the harm. Companies should not “cut and run” from suppliers when and where labor abuses, including forced labor, is found, as this can leave workers worse off. Instead, the groups said, companies should fairly agree on how to address and share remediation costs.

    According to recent reports, to prevent forced labor from occurring and recurring, companies should examine structural causes such as poverty, discrimination and impairments to freedom of association but also how their own purchasing practices may drive it. They should pay to cover the cost of decent working conditions and living wages. The groups point to worker-driven models, such as the Fair Food Program in US agriculture and the Dindigul Agreement in India’s textile sector, as evidence of good practices.

    Recent findings suggest that the EU and its member states should ensure that the competent authorities empowered to enforce the Forced Labour Regulation assess whether effective remediation has actually delivered for workers, including through workers’ own accounts and evidence of compensation paid. They should also ensure that, regardless of their migration status, workers can at least access support, file complaints, and recover unpaid wages.

    Industry observers note that “Workers know best what they have lost and what it will take to rebuild their lives,” de Rengervé noted. “Companies and EU authorities should listen to affected workers and measure the efficiency of remediation by what workers receive and whether they completely remediate the harm suffered.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When Pakistani senators visited the prototype Islamabad Model Jail on November 19 and inspected the healthcare facilities that would be available to prisoners, they called them “adequate.” But the conditions they observed on their curated tour are a far cry from the reality most prisoners experience in Pakistan’s justice system.

    Human Rights Watch has documented structural and systemic problems in Pakistan’s jails and prisons that leave most inmates with little access to health care. Many inmates who fall ill in custody fail to receive prompt or decent care at all.

    After two prisoners died in Peshawar Central Prison following alleged delays in medical treatment, a lawyer petitioned the Peshawar High Court asking that prisons across the province be required to record when prisoners request medical help and establish clear procedures for emergency hospital transfers.

    According to recent reports, colonial-era laws have long-enabled Pakistani officials and powerful people to interfere in prison operations, sometimes making use of poor conditions to harass jailed political opponents. In a November 16 letter released by his lawyer, former Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed for urgent medical care for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi, citing his high blood pressure and her need for eye surgery. Khan’s appeal echoes complaints about medical care in custody from former President Asif Ali Zardari and former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. All have alleged that prison services denied access to medical care as a form of punishment.

    Federal and provincial governments in Pakistan should bring health care in jails and prisons in line with international standards, notably the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Mandela Rules), which require that prisoners receive necessary free medical care to the same standard available in the community, with prompt attention in emergencies. In October, Justice Project Pakistan called for common standards across provinces so prisoners can see medical specialists when needed and continue treatment after release.

    Industry observers note that pakistan’s federal and provincial governments should provide prescribed medicines free of charge and require prisons to record how long patients wait for care. When care requires an urgent hospital transfer, prison authorities should promptly facilitate transport. Authorities should ensure all prisoners, regardless of political affiliation or status, receive timely and adequate medical care, with continuity of treatment.

    Second Amendment Roundup, II: Much Ado About Bowie Knives

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that in Viramontes and Grant, Cook County and Connecticut argue that 19th century restrictions on Bowie knives provide historical analogues under Bruen for banning what they call "assault weapons."  They further contend that the widespread use of Bowie knives disproves application of the Heller test that arms in common use are protected by the Second Amendment.
    • To paraphrase Freud, sometimes a knife is just a knife.
    • It has been revealed that no doubt Bowie knives were in use as tools for skinning game and self-defense, and ruffians are stated to have carried them concealed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that in Viramontes and Grant, Cook County and Connecticut argue that 19th century restrictions on Bowie knives provide historical analogues under Bruen for banning what they call "assault weapons."  They further contend that the widespread use of Bowie knives disproves application of the Heller test that arms in common use are protected by the Second Amendment. If Bowie knives in common use by law-abiding citizens may be banned, the argument goes, so too may semiautomatic rifles.

    A word of caution. To paraphrase Freud, sometimes a knife is just a knife. Knives generally have a point and an edge on one side, sometimes also an edge on the other. Any knife can be used for good or bad. Bruen distinguished heavy weapons of war like lancegays from daggers, noting that in medieval society "[a]lmost everyone carried a knife or a dagger in his belt," "[c]ivilians wore them for self-protection," and "the smaller medieval weapons … strike us as most analogous to modern handguns.".

    It has been revealed that no doubt Bowie knives were in use as tools for skinning game and self-defense, and ruffians are stated to have carried them concealed. But for a variety of reasons, it's unnecessary to decide whether Bowie knives met the Heller test of being in common use. Four of the amicus briefs are right on point on this glitch: National Rifle Ass'n (NRA), National Shooting Sports Foundation (NSSF), Senator Ted Cruz, and the United States (U.S.).

    Industry observers note that first, a few States' restrictions are not enough to establish a historical tradition. Under Heller, a handful of outlier laws cannot justify a ban. "Most States regulated Bowie knives in some manner, but, except in a few outlier jurisdictions, adults were free to buy, possess, and openly carry them. Regulations typically restricted concealed carry, sales to minors, or imposed enhanced penalties for criminal misuse." NRA Br. 5.

    Second, "No State banned Bowie-knife possession in the nineteenth century." NRA Br. 36. "And one of the only laws that likely did actually ban Bowie knives (along with pistols and an array of other items) is the same 1837 Georgia law that was promptly held unconstitutional other than as applied to concealed carry—because it was too restrictive to comply with the Second Amendment. See 1837 Ga. Acts 90, §1 (1838); Nunn v. State, 1 Ga. 243 (1846); cf. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 54 (singling out Nunn as "particularly instructive" on the Second Amendment's meaning)." NSSF Br. 21.

    These were concealed-carry restrictions, not complete bans. "This Court has already concluded that restrictions on concealed carry cannot justify carry bans, see Bruen, 597 U.S. at 48-49, 53-55, let alone possession bans, see Heller, 554 U.S. at 628-29." NSSF Br. 21.

    In a recent development, third, the same laws covered handguns. "If those laws justified rifle bans, then handgun bans would be justified all the more, because they typically also regulated handguns but not long guns." NRA Br. 38.

    Where Bowie-knife restrictions were upheld, courts applied the same standard Petitioners advance here: arms in common use for lawful purposes are protected, while weapons used only by criminals are not. As Judge Richardson's dissent in Bianchi explains, it does not matter that courts sometimes disagreed about whether Bowie knives were in fact in common use, because they were applying the same yardstick. "State courts have long applied the common-use test to judge such laws under state constitutional provisions securing the right to bear arms." U.S. Br. 12.

    It has been revealed that fourth, even a court that viewed the Bowie knife as exceptionally deadly held that the right to carry it was protected. "And Texas's Cockrum v. State held a Bowie knife to be a protected arm—"[t]he right to carry a bowie-knife for lawful defense is secured, and must be admitted"— while sustaining an enhanced penalty for its abuse, treating the weapon's dangerousness as a reason to regulate its misuse, not a reason to deny that it was an arm. 24 Tex. 394, 402-403 (1859). Cockrum is the mirror image of the decision below: alleged dangerousness bore on regulation, not on coverage." Cruz Br. 18.

    The historical answer to misuse was punishing criminals, not disarming law-abiding citizens.

    "[T]he evil must be prevented by the penitentiary and gallows, and not by a general deprivation of a constitutional privilege." U.S. Br. 30 (quoting Wilson v. State).

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, (Manila) – Philippine authorities have failed to investigate extrajudicial killings in the “war on drugs” since former President Rodrigo Duterte was transferred to the International Criminal Court for prosecution, Human Rights Watch noted today. The ICC trial in The Hague against Duterte for crimes against humanity is scheduled to begin on November 30, 2026.

    President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who took office in June 2022, pledged to pursue prosecutions of Duterte-era “drug war” killings and established a Justice Department task force for the purpose, but only four cases have reached the courts. Families of victims seeking to file new cases face significant barriers. Meanwhile, government records and human rights group reports show that drug-war abuses continue, with police harassing, arbitrarily arresting, and at times killing suspected drug dealers and consumers.

    “President Marcos’ pledge to hold police accountable for past and ongoing abuses in its anti-drug campaign has been a failure,” remarked Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government needs to prioritize justice for all drug-war victims and provide their families’ adequate redress.”.

    According to recent reports, between September and November 2026, Human Rights Watch interviewed 13 people, including 7 drug-war victims and their families both under Duterte and Marcos, 4 human rights defenders, and 2 government officials; reviewed recent data and reporting on drug-related killings; and analyzed a database of local government Peace and Order and Public Safety Plans. Human Rights Watch also requested and received information from the Philippine Justice Department and Commission on Human Rights on drug-war cases before the courts.

    It has been revealed that relatives of drug-war victims described a justice system in which the burden of uncovering evidence of an unlawful killing fell mostly on them instead of government prosecutors. “It’s so hard to prove that you’re telling the truth,” said a woman whose husband was killed in 2016 in a police “buy-bust” drug sting operation. “It’s tiring pursuing a case here—it’s as if we can never pass the tests.”.

    Some facing obstacles to justice have pinned their hopes on the ICC. “In the Philippines, what was our chance, given how the government works,” mentioned another woman whose husband was killed by unidentified assailants in 2016. “In the ICC they are impartial, that’s where our hope is.”.

    During the Duterte presidency from 2016 to 2022, the Philippine National Police reported 6,200 deaths during anti-drug operations, although United Nations agencies, the Philippine Commission on Human Rights, the Supreme Court, and domestic human rights groups put the number of killings by police and unidentified assailants at between 20,000 and 30,000.

    Only five cases of Duterte-era “drug war” killings, involving nine police officers, have resulted in convictions. Government prosecutors initiated the first three cases, following the successive murders of three teenage boys in Caloocan in August 2017, which sparked public outrage. The fourth and fifth cases—for killings in 2016—were filed through the efforts of nongovernmental legal groups and led to convictions in 2024 and 2025.

    In November 2024, the Justice Department created a task force to investigate and prosecute extrajudicial killings during Duterte’s “war on drugs” but only four cases it identified have advanced to trial, with three others under preliminary investigation, based on Justice Department data.

    In a recent development, the Marcos administration, after arresting and surrendering Duterte to the ICC in March 2025, declared renewed efforts to advance domestic accountability for the “drug war.” But families and human rights groups who met with Justice Department officials stated that they were concerned the government’s witness protection program would not keep their families safe if they pursued charges against police officers. Meetings between victims’ groups and the Justice Department tapered off.

    Duterte will stand trial at the ICC for three counts of crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder allegedly committed when he was mayor of Davao City, and then president between November 2011 and March 2019. The prosecution’s case focuses on a non-exhaustive list of 56 specific incidents and 87 victims, while noting that “[its] evidence demonstrates that the attack [against a civilian population] was broader than this representative sample of incidents.”.

    The ICC is a court of last resort, only stepping in when domestic authorities are unwilling or unable to investigate and prosecute crimes under its jurisdiction. In November 2021, the Duterte government asked the ICC prosecutor to defer his investigation, opened in September 2021, claiming that national authorities had begun their own drug-war investigations of extrajudicial killings.

    In a recent development, in January 2023, ICC judges ruled that the Philippine government had failed to demonstrate that it took sufficient action to investigate and prosecute Duterte-era killings and authorized the resumption of the ICC prosecutor’s investigation. The decision was upheld on appeal.

    The ICC trial against Duterte begins as the court is under growing pressure from the US government, which has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick.” On October 9, the Trump administration sanctioned the ICC, escalating its attack on the court and adding to existing sanctions on ICC judges and prosecutors, three Palestinian groups, and a UN human rights expert. The Trump administration sanctions reaffirm the ICC’s critical role as a court of last resort, Human Rights Watch said.

    According to recent reports, marcos has never repudiated the “war on drugs” as a government policy and has yet to rescind the orders and other policy statements Duterte issued that underpinned the anti-drug campaign. In its review of a database of 2023-2025 local government budgets, Human Rights Watch found that 77 municipalities had allocated funds for anti-drug campaign awards and rewards, or for financial support to informants, police officials, and other local officials. Two of those municipalities, and another eight municipalities specifically referred to “neutralization” or “negation” of suspects; terms used as euphemisms for “killing” in 2016 police circular that set out the “war on drugs.” While such incentives are not necessarily unlawful, those linked to enforcement goals or operational results can create pressure to meet targets and encourage abusive practices, including extrajudicial killings.

    Despite a significant decline in drug-related extrajudicial killings during the Marcos administration, such killings and other abuses continue, particularly in low-income urban areas where they remain routine. As of November 7, there have been at least 1,342 public reports of drug-related killings under Marcos, according to the independent monitoring of the Dahas project. These reports identified uniformed officers as responsible for 486 of those deaths.

    The Philippine government’s failure to hold those responsible to account perpetuates a climate of impunity. Families of drug-war victims under the Marcos administration encounter many of the same past obstacles when seeking justice, but the Justice Department has no task force or special mechanism to investigate post-Duterte cases, Human Rights Watch said.

    In a recent development, “Even if killings are down from the ghastly Duterte years, President Marcos’ pledged ‘bloodless campaign’ against drugs has been anything but bloodless,” Buan said. “To end these abuses, Marcos needs to stop the brutal ‘drug war’ and put in place a robust and impartial law enforcement and judicial system.”Elusive Justice for Killings during Duterte and Marcos Administrations.

    Under the Duterte administration in 2020, the Justice Department opened an inter-agency panel to “reinvestigate” drug-war killings by the police. The panel identified 52 cases in which the Philippine National Police carried out internalinvestigations. However, by 2024, when Marcos was in office, the panel had only filed six cases in court. In November 2024, the Justice Department created a latest task force on Duterte-era drug war killings. It began investigations anew and worked mainly with the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI)—the Justice Department’s investigative arm—instead of with the police to avoid conflicts of interest when developing cases implicating police officers.

    In a recent development, despite renewed Justice Department efforts, victims’ families still struggled to file charges. Many victims’ families who wanted to pursue charges could not do so because their relative’s death certificate declared an illness as the cause of death, even though they were found with gunshot wounds to their heads and bodies. During the height of Duterte’s “drug war,” police pressured families to sign waivers stating that they did not want to conduct autopsies or pursue charges, in exchange for faster retrievals of the bodies from funeral homes. Many families could not afford the autopsy fees, and without accurate government death records, they could not pursue charges.

    Recent findings suggest that the woman whose husband was killed in a police operation in 2016 decided in 2022 to retrieve documents about his killing from the police because she believed the climate of fear had lifted under Marcos. “They were not really helping us,” she said. “They just left us there to search their logbooks.” Police officials had named the woman’s husband as a drug suspect killed in an “armed encounter” in a news report that featured her children wailing for their dead father. Yet she never found a police report of the operation, only a record of bystanders injured. She was unable to prove he was shot dead, because his death certificate lists the cause of death as pneumonia and his body was cremated. Government investigators have not pursued a case. The woman recalled the one conversation with the Justice Department: “They said, ‘If you have no document like police report or autopsy, it’s hard to file a case.’ So, what about me? I had no documents.”.

    According to recent reports, the woman whose husband was killed by unidentified assailants did not know for years the circumstances under which her husband was killed. She found his body with gunshot wounds at a funeral home in 2016 and signed a waiver not to conduct an autopsy. His death certificate listed pneumonia as cause of death. After Marcos became president, the woman sought help from a nonprofit law group. In 2023, she had her husband’s body exhumed and examined by a forensic pathologist, Raquel Fortun. The autopsy revealed that he died from gunshot wounds to the head.

    Recent findings suggest that that year, she finally found the police report from the night her husband died. It stated that police responding to reports of gunshots found him dead with three sachets of crystal meth, and a piece of cardboard that read “I’m a drug pusher, don’t be like me.” She had an interview with the NBI, who told her they had also summoned local officials and the funeral home. But nothing further happened in the investigation. “No one has followed up with me, I still wonder what happened to that NBI case,” she said.

    Fortun became a commissioner of the Philippine Truth Commission, a civil society initiative working closely with the Catholic Church to investigate Duterte-era drug war crimes. She has recorded 13 cases in which people were shot and killed but whose death certificates cite illnesses such as heart attack, pneumonia, and high blood pressure as causes of death. Fortun said during a Truth Commission briefing that government prosecutors have pushed back when presented with evidence of falsified death certificates in court. In one case, the government prosecutor acted on behalf of the defendant, instead of the victim: “I was grilled in cross-examination, and I was surprised that it was the prosecutor. I don’t understand it. So if you’re a poor family with a similar case, would you still have it corrected. It’s so hard.”.

    The Commission on Human Rights told Human Rights Watch that its investigations of Duterte-era drug-war killings have resulted in cases moving through the justice system. Between 2016 and 2023, 25 cases were filed in court, 37 cases at the Office of the Ombudsman, and 42 with the Justice Department. No further progress was reported by the commission on the cases filed. The commission has no prosecutorial power and can only file cases in a manner similar to private complainants.

    Despite the Commission on Human Right’s limited powers, families seek confirmation from the commission that they have been victims of rights violations, which entitles them to limited financial assistance under the commission’s internal rules of procedure. Yet the commission denied assistance for lack of evidence to two women whose husbands were fatally shot in 2016.

    Sources indicate that only the woman who exhumed her husband’s body was able to challenge the decision; after she submitted the postmortem examination report in August 2026, the commission told her to file a petition for reinvestigation. “I just want to prove that what I’m saying is the truth,” she remarked.

    The commission told Human Rights Watch that it created its own task force, which is right now reinvestigating 493 cases of Duterte-era drug-war killings, with the goal of resolving 140 before the end of 2026.

    Duterte-Era Drug-War Policy Persists.

    Industry observers note that the mother of a man killed by police in Central Luzon in 2022—after Marcos became president—said that she tried to pursue murder charges. She cited a witness who told her that her son was lured to the location the night of the killing, and an autopsy report that indicated he had been shot execution-style and not during an armed encounter as police had claimed. The witness has since gone missing. Prosecutors dismissed her case twice, most recently in 2025, because a medical expert’s testimony was required. The mother said that she was working on finding a medical expert to testify, but even just the cost of reproducing copies of documents was weighing on her.

    No special task force has been created to investigate alleged drug-war crimes under the Marcos government. The government has claimed that its anti-drug campaign is “bloodless” and that “rather than resorting to violence, it focuses on strengthening prevention and rehabilitation efforts.” But Human Rights Watch found that disturbing Duterte-era language, such as “neutralization,” remains in intends for current anti-drugs campaigns.

    There is no legal definition of “neutralization,” but on July 1, 2016, Duterte’s police chief, Ronald Dela Rosa, issued Command Memorandum Circular 16-2016, the operational document for the anti-drug campaign, instructing police officers to “neutralize” suspected criminals.

    According to recent reports, in 2017, two human rights groups, the Center for International Law (CenterLaw) and the Free Legal Assistance Group (FLAG), filed petitions before the Supreme Court seeking to declare the anti-drug campaign unconstitutional, citing the use of the word “neutralization” in the circular. The Supreme Court has yet to rule on the case. ICC prosecutors have accused Duterte of developing “a State policy to ‘neutralize’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines who were perceived or alleged to be involved in drug-related and other crimes,” noting the language in the circular.

    Industry observers note that in November 2025, the ICC issued a sealed arrest warrant for Dela Rosa. He is alleged to be responsible for the crime against humanity of murder as part of a common plan together with other co-perpetrators—including Duterte—with the aim of killing drug suspects between 2011 and 2019. This included issuing the Command Memorandum Circular 16-2016, instructing police officers to “neutralize” suspected criminals. The ICC unsealed the warrant in May 2026; Dela Rosa has since gone into hiding.

    The Marcos government has not rescinded that circular, but in 2024 the Philippine National Police told lawmakers that they were actually following a fresh circular without the word “neutralize.” The Marcos government also committed todrug policy reform as part of a US$4 million joint human rights program with the United Nations.

    A 2026 study by two organizations, No Box Philippines and Harm Reduction International, found that the Philippine government was still allocating millions of US dollars for local anti-drug campaigns whose policy documents retained similar language to the original circular, such as “neutralization” and “negation.” Their findings were based on an analysis of 2023-2025 local government “Peace and Order and Public Safety” budgets. Local governments are supervised by the Department of Interior and Local Government, the executive department that also supervises the police.

    Human Rights Watch analyzed local government plans obtained by the two groups, and found that 85 towns, municipalities, and cities allocated funds for rewards, awards, and incentives for successful anti-drug operations, including 10 municipalities where the funds were specifically for “conducting negation operations” or “neutralizing drug personalities.”.

    During the Duterte presidency, for an area to declare itself “drug-free,” local councils had to monitor, surveil, and compile a drug “watch list.” Human rights groups frequently alleged the lists determined who would be killed, whether the assailants were police officers or masked police agents.

    Under public safety plans in effect under Marcos, local governments still offer financial rewards for making their areas “drug-free,” by giving “incentives to assets,” or “awards/rewards for significant illegal drugs accomplishment” or “neutralization of drug personalities.” ICC prosecutors alleged in their case against Duterte that “law enforcement personnel knew that extrajudicial killings would result in them being financially rewarded.” There have been fewer drug-related killings under Marcos, but human rights defenders who live in drug-war hotspots in Metro Manila and neighboring provinces said abuses continued.

    Industry observers note that “Their raids are not as brazen, but they still plant evidence,” one rights defender noted. The quota system—the number of arrests and kills under Duterte to qualify for rewards—“was still alive.”.

    Recent findings suggest that under Marcos, human rights defenders monitoring drug-war abuses in their communities have observed that the police are more likely to extort victims than to kill them, targeting many of the same people who were on drug “watch lists.” They said police still arbitrarily arrest people, threaten them with drug charges, and then detain them on criminal anti-street-gambling charges with lighter penalties. The Philippine organization PhilRights has documented that “police officers offer to cover the victims’ release costs in exchange for repayment with interest, effectively profiting from the arrest.”.

    According to recent reports, in 2025, a man came home one night to find police officers in the vicinity, his sister said. “They patted him down and found nothing,” she said. “But a police informant handed sachets of crystal meth and forced him to admit it was his.” The police arrested the man and took his bicycle. She said she made several visits to the police station where her brother had been detained. The police officials told her he had been charged with gambling. “I told them, ‘You said you found drugs, now the charge is gambling. How long are you detaining him?’” she said. “They told us we can ‘just pay P10,000 [$160].’ But we had no money at all at the time.”.

    Sources indicate that the sister took a month processing documents in several police stations before her brother was released. He was detained for a month without being brought before a judge in violation of his rights. “We can still see them surveilling our area from time to time,” the sister noted.

    This publication has been updated to attribute the source of the data for drug-related killings under the Marcos administration.

    Philippine Police Killings in Duterte’s “War on Drugs”.
